The Chatooga River, located about 5 miles west of the proposed project, has been designated as a National Wild and Scenic River.
The Corps of Engineers' Hartwell Reservoir is located about 40 miles south of the proposed project. This 56,000-acre facility in South Carolina and Georgia is now the most popular recreation area within the 50-mile region surrounding the project. There are over 70 developed public use areas circling the reservoir, including 3 State parks and 4 commercial marinas; some 81 boat ramps and 778 camping units have been developed. Over 6 million recreation visits were recorded at this reservoir in 1973 (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 1973 and 1974).
2.1.3 Topography, Physiography, Geology, and Ground Water
The Bad Creek pumped storage site is located within the Blue Ridge Geologic Province near the western margin of South Carolina. The topographic expression of the project area may be characterized as mature uplands which have been deeply dissected by young drainages. These drainages, having a somewhat irregular dendritic pattern and a steep gradient, have caused widespread, unchecked erosion over a sizeable area.
The rocks in this area are believed to be Pre-Cambrian in age, being part of the North American continental shield. They are typically gneissic, ranging from resistant granitic varieties to those that are very soft and schistose. Geologically, they have been mapped as two formations, the Toxaway Gneiss and the Tallulah Falls formations. Being ancient metamorphic rocks, they have experienced numerous periods of intensive deformation. They are folded, faulted, crushed, and sheared, all of which has accelerated their weathering and decomposition to maximum depths of 100 feet in certain areas.
The Brevard Fault Zone, which extends from Virginia to Alabama, is the major structural feature in the region. This zone crosses the upper reaches of Lake Jocassee but does not affect the proposed project. It is about 2 miles from the Bad Creek Reservoir at its closest point. This zone of major faulting has been inactive throughout the recent geologic record; however, there have been very small seismic events recorded in the area in the past few years. The greatest magnitude was 3.2 on the Richter scale in November 1975, but the majority of micro shocks have magnitudes less than 2.0. The events are being monitored by the licensee in conjunction with the State Geologic Survey and the University of South Carolina.
